question.:question/problem: The point $P$ has polar coordinates $(2,{210}^{∘}).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ x & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡({210}^{∘}) \\ x & =2\cdot -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x & =-\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ y & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡({210}^{∘}) \\ y & =2\cdot -\frac{1}{2} \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-\sqrt{3},-1).$

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡({60}^{∘}) \\  & =4\sqrt{3}(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡({60}^{∘}) \\  & =4\sqrt{3}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(2\sqrt{3},6).$
